vignette:
David speaks of his life in two distinct tenses: before and after the assault. Before, he was the principal of Northwood High, a man who moved through the familiar halls with an easy authority. He knew the names of nearly all 900 students, the squeak of the third stall in the boys' bathroom, and the precise angle of the sun that hit his desk at 3:00 p.m. His world was orderly, predictable, and safe. He was, in his own words, “the captain of the ship.”

The "after" began ten months ago on a cold Tuesday night in the school’s near-empty parking lot. He had just wrapped up a contentious parent meeting regarding a student’s long-term suspension. The father, a large man whose frustration had been simmering all evening, followed him out. The conversation, already frayed, quickly unraveled. David remembers the smell of stale coffee on the man’s breath and the glint of the overhead lamp on his glasses. He remembers saying, “The decision is final,” and turning toward his car. The first shove sent him off-balance, his briefcase skittering across the asphalt. The second sent him to the ground, the impact knocking the wind from his lungs. He felt a sharp, radiating pain in his shoulder as his head hit the pavement. He lay there, disoriented, as the man stood over him, shouting words that have since blurred into a single, menacing hum.

The physical injuries—a mild concussion and a dislocated shoulder—healed within a few months. The rest did not. At first, he tried to power through it, returning to work after only a week. He told everyone, including his wife, Sarah, that he was fine, just a bit shaken up. But the captain was no longer steady at the helm.

He now finds himself avoiding the west parking lot, taking a longer route to a spot on the far side of the school each morning. He delegates any disciplinary meetings involving angry parents to his vice-principal, citing a need to focus on “administrative oversight.” The excuse feels flimsy even to him, a betrayal of the hands-on leader he once was. His office, once a sanctuary, now feels like a fishbowl. He keeps the blinds angled down and often startles violently when a student knocks on his door without first being announced by his secretary. The familiar, chaotic energy of the school day—a locker slamming, a sudden shout in the hallway, the bell’s jarring ring—now puts his entire nervous system on high alert, a tightness blooming in his chest that takes hours to subside.

Sleep offers little respite. He often jolts awake, heart hammering, the sensation of falling replaying in his mind. He’ll lie there in the dark, staring at the ceiling, cataloging every sound in the house while Sarah sleeps beside him. He feels a profound distance from her, as if he’s watching his own life through soundproof glass. She’ll ask him what’s wrong, and he’ll say, “Just thinking about work,” because the truth feels too heavy to voice. The truth is, he feels a constant, humming sense of dread. He looks at the faces of parents at school events and feels a prickle of suspicion, a silent assessment of threat. The world, and especially the school he once loved, no longer feels safe. He feels broken, a fraud in a suit and tie, and is terrified that it is only a matter of time before one of his teachers or, worse, one of his students, sees the cracks.
